new_entities.name: Early mobilization for ICU-acquired weakness prevention
new_entities.description: Structured early mobilization or rehabilitation in the ICU to limit weakness and muscle loss during critical illness.

new_entities.name: Muscle preservation
new_entities.description: Maintenance of muscle mass or muscle strength during illness, hospitalization, or recovery.

edges.effect_quant: Meta-analyses show lower ICU-acquired weakness with early mobilization, including RR 0.60 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.90) and OR 0.22 (95% CI 0.14 to 0.35), though one newer RCT improved mobilization level without changing measured muscle strength.
edges.population: critically ill adults admitted to intensive care units
edges.mechanism: Early mobilization counters immobilization-driven catabolism, neuromuscular disuse, and the rapid loss of contractile activity that drives ICU-acquired weakness. Even when strength gains are hard to capture over a short ICU stay, earlier activation may still preserve enough function to reduce downstream weakness and dependence.
edges.summary: The best aggregate evidence supports early mobilization as a muscle-preserving strategy in critical care, mainly through lower ICU-acquired weakness and better functional recovery at discharge. The signal is not universal in every individual trial, but the pooled evidence still favors early rehabilitation over routine bed rest or delayed mobilization.
edges.caveats: Interventions range from passive mobilization to active exercise and walking protocols, and studies use different strength and function endpoints. Short ICU stays and severe illness can make true muscle preservation difficult to measure precisely, so some trials show functional gains without clear changes on strength scales.
